children.text: Standing in the heart of Sariaya town in Quezon Province, the Church of Saint Francis of Assisi is a Baroque brick church completed in 1748. It is a diocesan shrine housing Santo Cristo de Burgos, an image regarded as miraculous, and can be visited as a day trip from Manila.

The Saint Francis of Assisi Parish Church is a Roman Catholic church in the poblacion (town proper) of Sariaya, Quezon Province, under the Diocese of Lucena. Its formal name is the Saint Francis of Assisi Parish Church, but locals usually just call it Sariaya Church, and it is also known as the Diocesan Shrine of Santo Cristo de Burgos after the image enshrined inside. Sariaya lies about
120km
south of Manila, and the Maharlika Highway (N1), which runs from Manila toward the Bicol region, passes through the town center, so it is also an easy stop on the way to the southern provinces.
The church's history goes back to the early Spanish colonial period. According to records, the first church was built in
, with further churches raised in 1605 and 1641. In 1703 the town is said to have been moved to Lumangbayan (meaning "old town"). After earthquakes and floods destroyed the church in
, residents relocated to the present site, and the current church was completed in

during the tenure of the Spanish friars Fr. Martin de Talavera and Fr. Joaquin Alapont. The Sariaya Tourism Council says the church was built with free labor from local residents during the colonial era. In 1938 the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) installed a historical marker, and Wikipedia lists the church as an Important Cultural Property (ICP). The walls are red brick faced with adobe slabs and plastered on the outside, and the style is classified as Barn Style Baroque. The plan is cruciform, the transept has side altars, and the buttresses also serve as part of the side walls. The four-storey belfry still holds old bells, and its ground floor is the old baptistery. The roof, originally of brick tiles, was replaced with galvanized iron in 1947, and the convent attached to the left side of the church was completed in
under Fr. Policarpio Trinidad.

What makes this church a beloved pilgrimage site is its image. The patron is Saint Francis of Assisi, but visitors and the faithful know the church best for Santo Cristo de Burgos (Mahal na Señor), a crucified Christ believed to be miraculous, and pilgrims come from far away to see it. Local accounts say the image was a gift from King Philip V to the people of Lumangbayan and that it survived the disasters of 1743, which was regarded as a miracle. Another legend says that the men carrying the image found it too heavy to lift at one spot, and took that as a sign to build the church there. On September 14, 2007, during the town fiesta, Bishop Emilio Marquez of Lucena formally declared the church the Diocesan Shrine of the Mahal na Señor, Santo Cristo de Burgos.

For travelers, Sariaya Church is an easy stop, with no long entrance lines and no lengthy itinerary. Rather than seeing the church alone, I recommend walking it together with the heritage houses and plaza in the town center as a half-day route that captures Quezon's colonial atmosphere. Sariaya is about
10km
from Lucena, with Mount Banahaw to the north and Tayabas Bay to the south, so it also leads naturally into a trip combining mountains and sea.
This colonial-era church combines thick walls of red brick and adobe slabs, a cruciform plan, and a barn-shaped roof. The present building was completed in
, so it has watched over the town on this spot for more than 270 years.

blocks.title: The Santo Cristo de Burgos image

children.text: This crucified Christ image, known as miraculous, is now enshrined behind the retablo. The church also holds an 18th-century replica of the image. You can see the faithful, and travelers too, praying quietly.

The four-storey belfry still holds old bells, and the ground floor houses the old baptistery. Looking up at the belfry from the front of the church, you can tell right away which is the tallest building in town.

Near the altar stands an old retablo, and the two side altars in the transept hold old saint images. The interior is dimly lit and very quiet, so please take care not to disturb other worshippers when taking photos.

The convent courtyard has a devotional park with a Last Supper replica, a Lourdes grotto, and candle shrines. Outdoor installations around the church are said to include statues of Jesus on the cross, the Stations of the Cross, and the Archangel Michael slaying the devil.
The Museo ng Debosyon at Buhay (Museum of Devotion and Life) displays church implements, relics, and old photographs. Opening hours can change, so it is safest to check with the parish office.

blocks.title: Linking up with the Sariaya heritage houses

children.text: Near the church stand the Enriquez-Gala mansion, the Gala-Rodriguez house, and the house of Catalino and Luisa Rodriguez, called Villa Sariaya. These are the three mansions marked by the National Historical Institute (NHI) in 2008, and you can tour them on foot together with the church.

items.title: Day trip from Manila
items.subtitle: From the church and heritage houses on to Lucena

children.text: Take a bus bound for Lucena or the Bicol region from a bus terminal in southern Manila. Tell the driver or conductor in advance that you want to get off at Sariaya town proper (poblacion).
Arrive in Sariaya town proper. Arrival times vary widely depending on road conditions. The church stands in the town center and is easy to spot.
Look at the church facade and belfry from outside first, then go in when no Mass is under way and quietly view the Santo Cristo de Burgos image.
Visit the devotional park in the convent courtyard and the Franciscan Museum. Check locally whether the museum is open.
Walk the heritage house street and the plaza on foot, and have lunch in town.
If you have time left, continue to Lucena or Tayabas for your next stop. Catch your return bus before it gets late.
The church visit alone takes about
1–2 hours
. A realistic plan is to spend the rest of the time on the town's heritage houses and a meal.

items.title: Two-day Quezon heritage route
items.subtitle: From Sariaya to Lucban and Tayabas

children.text: Travel from Manila to Sariaya and tour the church and the heritage houses.
Move on to Lucena, check in, and look around the city.
Head to Tayabas and Lucban to see the old churches and town atmosphere. In May you could also time your visit to the Pahiyas Festival.
Lodging fills up early during festivals, so book ahead.

From southern Manila (the Pasay, Cubao, and Alabang areas), take a long-distance bus bound for Lucena or the Bicol region and get off at Sariaya town proper. Because the Maharlika Highway (N1) runs through the town, Bicol-bound buses often stop in Sariaya town proper.
The distance from Manila is about
120km
. In heavy traffic it can take
3–4 hours
or more, so an early start is best. Fares and bus companies change often, so check at the terminal.
Some direct buses do not stop in Sariaya, so be sure to confirm "Sariaya drop-off" when you board.

Take the SLEX and STAR Tollway, then head south on the N1 (Maharlika Highway) to reach Sariaya town proper (poblacion). The town center is narrow and parking is limited, so check locally for roadside or nearby parking near the church.

items.title: By jeepney from Lucena or Tayabas

children.text: From Lucena or Tayabas, take a jeepney to Sariaya town proper and ask to be dropped off near the church. The church stands in the town center and is easy to spot.
The church, plaza, and heritage houses are all clustered in the town center and can be reached on foot. For longer distances take a tricycle, but agree on the fare before you ride.

The church is an open parish church all year round, so the season matters little, but for outdoor travel and strolling the town the dry season from November to May is more comfortable. It gets hot at midday, so it is better to walk in the morning or toward sunset.

The town fiesta is reported to be held around mid-September. A news report says the 2007 shrine declaration took place at the September 14 town fiesta, but check the latest parish announcements to see whether the date is the same every year. During the Agawan Festival on May 15, honoring San Isidro Labrador, the town gets very crowded, which is good for photos and sightseeing but means you should allow plenty of travel time.

Sariaya town proper has a few small lodgings and eateries, but Lucena, the provincial capital, offers far more choice. It is convenient to base yourself in Lucena and make a daytime trip to Sariaya. Quezon is a province where coconut dishes and spicy Bicol-style cooking are easy to find, so it is also worth trying local food at a town eatery.

Small eateries, bakeries, and shops cluster in the town center near the church. Business conditions change often, so no specific shop names are given here; I suggest choosing a place where plenty of people are eating.
A church is a place where worshippers pray. Please refrain from walking around inside and taking photos during Mass.
Neat clothing that covers the shoulders and knees is best. Take off your hat indoors.
Mass times and museum opening hours can change, so check parish announcements before you visit.
For a day trip from Manila, leave early in the morning and check the return bus times in advance.
The church and the heritage houses are within walking distance, so see them together in one go.
During the hottest hours, rest for a while in the church courtyard and bring water and a hat.
Combining it with Lucban during the Pahiyas Festival in May lets you feel Quezon's traditional atmosphere more deeply.
This is a place of faith, so be quiet during Mass and prayer, and avoid flash photography and loud talking near the image and altar.
Mass and museum opening hours and admission rules could not be confirmed. Check parish announcements before you visit.
The Maharlika Highway is very congested on weekends and holidays, especially during Holy Week. Allow plenty of travel time.
Watch for crowds and pickpockets in the town center, and wear your bag in front of you.
There is no fixed tricycle fare chart in town, so bargain before you ride.
Getting around becomes inconvenient after dark, so take care not to miss your return bus.
The provincial capital of Quezon, about
10km
from Sariaya. It is the best-equipped base for lodging, food, and transport.
